rows.evidence: Q1: Section 3 (Case analysis), Sections 3.2-3.4, Figs. 7, 9, Tables 3-5 - the authors run their own case study in a 13 ha jujube orchard in Alar, Xinjiang (2021), comparing yields under their management scheme versus traditional management, comparing UAV-based yield estimates with harvested yields, and comparing economic benefit of two harvesting paths.
rows.notes: The study does not use soil moisture sensors, does not monitor soil moisture, and does not report any irrigation adjustments. Space information is obtained from a DJI UAV (fruit and panoramic images) and agrometeorological satellites (temperature, moisture, precipitation, wind etc.). The only mention of sensors is 'sensor networks' and 'drip irrigation pipe networks' as obstacles that harvesting machinery should avoid (Section 2.4, Section 4). Fruit quality (average selling price, Table 3) is linked to harvest timing and weather-driven path planning, not to irrigation. The field-management yield comparison (Scheme 1 vs 2, Fig. 7) is an unquantified yield difference attributed to the integrated UAV/satellite scheme generally. So the study provides no evidence on soil sensors enabling irrigation adjustments for fruit quality; the cited technology differs from the one in the passage.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a UAV/satellite 'space information' scheme for jujube orchard management, yield estimation and harvest path planning; it contains no soil sensor or irrigation experiment. Results are mostly qualitative (Fig. 7 unquantified) or single-run comparisons without dispersion measures.
